title: Expert starvation and crossover sweep: Llama/Mistral/Qwen long-context notes
summary: Notes from a focused sweep investigating expert starvation and cross-model handoff effects on p95/p99 latency for long-context workloads across Llama, Mistral and Qwen families. Experiments probe whether starvation is scheduling-related (serialization/handshake), KV staleness, or PCIe/DMA backpressure during prefetch and handoff.
environment: Testbed: 2x H100-80GB (NVLink), 1x A100-80GB (PCIe) for cross-arch experiments. Driver: NVIDIA 535.x, CUDA 12.2, nsight-systems v2024.3. Serving runtime: commit 9b3aefc (routing + prefetch refactor), build tag: v0.12.4-experiments. Models: llama-2-13b (fp16), mistral-instruct-7b (fp16), qwen-14b (int8-quant-sim). Long context token lengths: 2k, 8k, 32k. MoE config used: 64 experts, top-2 gating, expert capacity factor tuned to 1.0/1.5 in different runs.
experiments:
Run list (synthetic workload + real prompts):
1) Synthetic uniform token stream with repeated prefix to exercise cache reuse. Command: ./scripts/run_sweep.sh --model llama-2-13b --tokens 8192 --tps 8 --concurrency 4 --trace nvts
2) Cross-arch handoff: route 40% qwen -> mistral by policy to force redispatch and KV transfer. Command: ./tools/route_stresser.py --from qwen-14b --to mistral-7b --ratio 0.4 --duration 1800
3) Expert starvation probe: same input across MoE models with varying expert capacity (0.75,1.0,1.5) and top-k gating. Use microbench: ./bench/moe_starve.py --experts 64 --topk 2 --warmup 200 --measure p95,p99
4) DMA pressure capture: run nsys profile during a cross-host eviction event: nsys profile --output cross_handoff --trace=openacc,cuda,osrt ./bin/serve_e2e --workload cross_handoff.json
Notes: each run repeated 5 times, restart runtime between capacity changes to avoid kernel selection carryover.
observations:
High level:
- p50 stable across models; p95/p99 spikes correlate with redispatch events when routing crosses model families (qwen <-> mistral).
- When expert capacity factor = 0.75 we saw clear tail amplification: p99 increased by 2.2x vs capacity 1.5 for same throughput.
- NVLink host (H100 pair) reduced p95 of cross-model handoffs by ~30% compared to PCIe-only path (A100). However, p99 still present due to scheduling stalls in expert handshake.
- KV cache hit-rate drop from ~72% to ~51% during handoff bursts; each cache miss incurred average extra 8-14ms for remote KV prefetch/dma.
- NSYS traces show frequent short (~20-80us) gaps where GPU kernel queues empty while CPU-side routing logic waits on gated aggregation locks. These gaps produce serialization cascades under high concurrency.
- BPFtrace on host shows repeated wakeups (~1.8k/sec) by routing worker threads coinciding with p99 events; CPU sched latency peaked at 6-12ms in worst runs.
Numeric examples (representative):
run: llama-13b tokens=8192, concurrency=4 -> p50 32ms, p95 78ms, p99 210ms
run: qwen->mistral handoff (NVLink) -> p50 40ms, p95 95ms, p99 260ms
run: qwen->mistral handoff (PCIe) -> p50 46ms, p95 135ms, p99 410ms
Observation: gap between p95 and p99 often corresponds to a handful of requests that hit both cache miss + gating-serialization simultaneously.
root_causes_and_hypotheses:
1) Handshake serialization: gating aggregation (top-2 selection + capacity accounting) currently uses a single per-batch lock; when many sessions target overlapping experts this becomes a bottleneck and yields CPU-thread wakeup spikes. Hypothesis supported by BPFtrace wakeup correlation and nsight 'idle gaps'.
2) KV staleness amplification: during cross-model handoffs, the target model expects different tokenization/prefixing alignment, causing more cache misses and larger delta in prefetched KV sizes -> more PCIe/DMA traffic which amplifies stalls on PCIe hosts.
3) PCIe DMA queuing: A100(PCIe) shows DMA queue saturation when several large KV prefetches coincide; NVLink reduces host-to-host transfer overhead but cannot fix master-thread serialization.
4) Scheduling affinity: worker threads handling gating and serialization are running on non-isolated cores in our test VMs; scheduler preemption worsens tail.
Evidence: nsight timeline + perf show CPU syscall and lock contention during p99 windows; nvlink runs reduce DMA time but not lock time.
mitigation_attempts:
Tried quick patches (all in runtime branch 'moe-fast-fix'):
- Replaced per-batch lock with sharded locks (16 shards) for gating aggregation: reduced p99 by ~18% in small runs but not elimination.
- Added eager KV prefetch hints for cross-model handoff policy: improved cache hit by ~10%, p95 down 12% but p99 unchanged.
- Increased expert capacity factor to 1.5: reduced tail but increased average GPU memory by ~6GB.
- Offloaded gating aggregation to a dedicated pinned CPU thread set (isolcpus) which reduced scheduler latency spikes; p99 improved ~25% in NVLink runs but only 12% on PCIe runs.
- Disabled cross-model routing policy in a control run: tails disappeared but throughput dropped ~7% (expected).
recommended_next_steps:
Short term (next week):
- Roll gated sharded-locks + dedicated pinned worker thread prototype to canary pool for more realistic traffic.
- Instrument gating to capture per-expert queue lengths and per-request wait-time: add lightweight telemetry (histograms) to routing pipeline.
- Add eviction-aware KV prefetch scheduler that sequences large prefetches to avoid DMA queue storms on PCIe hosts.
Medium term (2-6 weeks):
- Rework gating aggregation algorithm to be lock-free (per-thread append + reduce) or use RCU-like pattern. Prototype on small scale.
- Explore hybrid handoff: copy minimal token metadata in routing vector to allow quick speculative KV rehydrate instead of full prefetch.
- Add host-level QoS: pin routing worker threads to cores and reserve CPU bandwidth for routing under high load.
Open questions:
- Can we adjust model tokenization alignment heuristics to improve KV reuse across model families?
- Cost tradeoffs for persistent larger KV allocation vs. dynamic prefetch complexity.
